text: Jurong Island: Seven Islands into One
Almost every Singaporean depends on Jurong Island, and almost none will ever set foot on it.

It is seven, joined by twenty years of reclamation into a single chemical fortress — and before the refineries, those seven islands held fishing villages whose headman's account of the strait is where this story has to start.

Ismail bin Mohd Ali, who had been penghulu, village head, of Pulau Ayer Merbau and the islands around it, explained the name by counting nine islands clustered there: Ayer Merbau, Ayer Chawan, Sakra, Bakau, Seraya, Merlimau, Meskol, Pesek and Mesemut Laut.
A British War Office map of 1939 shows fourteen islands in the strait, not nine.

"Ayer" means water, and marks the islands with fresh water on them: of Ayer Merbau's well, Ismail the penghulu said, "Even though it was shallow, the well never ran dry, and during the dry season, residents from nearby islands would come there to collect water."

In 1968 the government acquired the whole of Pulau Ayer Chawan and leased it to Esso, which paid for reclamation that grew the island from 0.73 to 1.54 square kilometres and built a 200 million Singapore dollars refinery on it.
One group of islanders was resettled three times over — from Pulau Samulun to Pulau Merlimau for the building of Jurong Port, then to Tanjong Keling, and finally into HDB flats in Jurong.

On the 25th of October 1988, at about half past one in the afternoon, fire broke out at an SRC naphtha storage tank on Pulau Merlimau — a 120,000-barrel tank whose jammed floating roof was under repair.
The work finished on the 25th of September 2009, twenty years ahead of schedule.

Beneath Banyan Basin, 130 metres under the seabed, five rock caverns — each 27 metres high, 20 metres wide and 340 metres long — hold 1.47 million cubic metres of crude oil, condensate, naphtha and gas oil.
The Singapore LNG terminal — decided in 2006, built for 1.7 billion Singapore dollars — began commercial operations on the 7th of May 2013 and was officially opened the following February.
In 2001 Jurong Island was gazetted a protected area, and it remains one.
The island built for oil is being retooled, carefully, for what comes after oil.
The penghulu's nine islands were really fourteen, and are now one — and the one is an island almost nobody will ever see.
